newsitem.title: USA: Bonds, stocks tumble after employment, manufacturing data.
newsitem.headline: Bonds, stocks tumble after employment, manufacturing data.

text.p: The bond market tumbled and the stock market slumped Friday after two surprisingly strong economic reports triggered fears that the Federal Reserve would raise interest rates in a bid to pre-empt inflation.
Expectations of rising interest rates pushed the dollar to almost an eight-year high against the German mark. Gasoline prices rose sharply on refinery disruptions in Europe.

The Dow Jones industrial average fell about 120 points during the session but regained much of the ground it lost and closed off 28.57 points at 8,194.04. The Nasdaq Composite rose 0.52 to a record 1,594.33.

The economic data worried the inflation-sensitive bond market, where the benchmark 30-year Treasury plunged 2-1/32, or $20.3125 on a $1,000 bond, raising its yield to 6.45 percent from 6.30 percent. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
The one-two punch began with the Labour Department's employment report and was followed by the National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) index, analysts said.
The Labour Department said the unemployment rate fell to 4.8 percent in July, the lowest in nearly 25 years, and the economy added 316,000 jobs, stronger than forecasts.
The NAPM report showed industrial activity and prices paid by manufacturers both registered unexpectedly sharp rises last month.
Analysts said the economic data revived the financial community's lurking fears of inflation -- and the prospect of an interest rate hike by the Fed to head it off.
Following the reports, investors immediately began selling shares, intent on cashing in on some of the market's dizzying gains.

"The image I use is that of a forest that hasn't experienced a fire in a very long time," said Charlie Crane, chief market strategist at Key Asset Management. "You get one spark and suddenly you have a blaze on your hands."
The Fed, the nation's central bank, raised short-term rates in March, the first increase in more than two years, but has held them steady since.

The reports and prospect of higher interest rates had the opposite effect on the dollar, which hit a high of 1.8665 marks, a level not seen since November 1989. The dollar's rise was also fuelled by concern about Europe's sluggish economy and uncertainty about the planned single currency.
In late trading, the dollar stood at 1.8628 marks, up from 1.8385 late Thursday.
The Japanese yen benefited from the mark's weakness and the dollar ended little changed at 118.39 yen vs. 118.65 yen Thursday.
In commodity markets, gasoline rose on the prospect that European refinery disruptions would hold up cargoes of gasoline slated for the United States in coming weeks.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, gasoline for September delivery rose 2.27 cents to 65.07 cents a gallon and set a life-of-contract high during the day.
Overseas, the FTSE index fell 8.2 points to 4,899.3 on the London market. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average tumbled 527.05 points, or 2.6 percent to 19,804.38.
